items.question: How do you see the significance of your behavior-cloning paper built around a Franka Panda arm?

items.answer: Our paper was, in essence, very simple. What we really showed was very simple: BC works. On a Franka Panda arm, we built a force-controlled teleoperation setup that made teleoperation extremely, extremely smooth. Then we built the entire pipeline from data collection through behavior cloning. We made a lot of arbitrary choices. For example, we decided to put a wrist camera on the robot—why not? No one was doing wrist cameras then, so we did one. We decided to use ResNet-18 as an encoder—why not? And then we used something called Spatial... I think it was a spatial softmax—Spatial-softmax layer—why not? Then we added an RNN. An RNN because we need history—why not? Everything was something we just came up with off the tops of our heads, and somehow it worked. It could really learn a great many behaviors we had never seen on robots before. For example, a very real task lasting 30 seconds, at 1x speed with no acceleration: pull out an oven tray, put something into the oven, close the oven, and put the tray back. When you do BC, you worry the paper will not get accepted.

items.question: Why did you find Meta's Project Aria glasses suitable for collecting EgoMimic's human manipulation data?
items.object: Meta's Project Aria glasses as EgoMimic's data-collection platform
items.answer: At first, we used Oculus—VR, right?—with a Leap Motion mounted on it. We built that system, then found that it worked very poorly because calibration was extremely unstable. You can imagine, there was one camera that could collect hand data, while video data came from another camera, and the VR headset was used to localize where your head was. So I had to calibrate all three things into the same coordinate frame. The gap there was very large. After struggling with it for several weeks, we felt it was too difficult. Then, as it happened, some colleagues were working on Meta's Ego4D. They had something called Project Aria, glasses made by Meta. Those glasses perfectly met all our needs: they could estimate hand state. That is, I could estimate the positions of all ten fingers. The glasses could localize themselves, so I knew where my head was, and they could simultaneously capture first-person RGB video data. We said, why do we not use this? We got it, and then the project began to go much more smoothly on the data-collection side. But as one of the earliest—perhaps the first—projects to really use this for robot learning, we hit many, many pitfalls. By the end, Meta had essentially become our dedicated support. Their entire team opened a P0, the highest-priority level, for us: all our support requests became P0 when they reached them. Altogether, it took about four or five months to get the data-collection side working—to get it working with Meta's Aria glasses.

items.question: Why did you want EgoMimic's robot to have a more human-like body?

items.question: How do you understand the limitations of teleoperation data for robot learning?
items.object: Teleoperation data and gaps within a robot platform
items.answer: This may have been a gradual change. But by the later stages of the project, I had a very strong thought: if you look at teleoperation data, teleoperation data itself is not perfect either. Every layer of every system introduces something. Let me give a simple example. Suppose I collect teleoperation data on a robot, then slightly change that robot's low-level controller—say, I adjust its gain just a little. The whole system reacts completely differently when you send it a control command. So even within a robot platform itself there can be a large gap.

items.question: How do you break down the problem of a robot or person interacting with the world?
items.object: Three subproblems of embodied interaction with the world
items.answer: Broadly, I think there are three parts. If you think of a robot or a person interacting with the human world, you can divide it into three subproblems. First is how you want the world to change. Second is how an embodied agent causes those changes in the world—for example, I want to pick up this cup or push it forward five centimeters. Third is what kind of control signals the embodiment itself uses to produce those movements—for example, how much force my motors need.

items.question: How do you distinguish the aspects of acting on the world that robots can learn from human video?
items.object: What robots can learn from human video
items.answer: Once you remove who caused those changes, there is no difference at all between humans and machines in how the world changes, provided your robot is capable enough to do it. The second layer can also be learned. For example, if I have a robot with a five-finger dexterous hand whose manipulation space is not so different from a human's and whose applicable force is also similar, then I can roughly learn the second type as well: how an embodiment can affect the world—roughly where to push, or where to grasp a cup to lift it. But the third layer is extremely, extremely hard to learn from human video: how to make an embodiment produce these actions. For example, an extreme example is throwing a ball. Exactly how a robot throws a ball is a very, very difficult problem, because you need to make every joint produce enough force to throw the ball along such a trajectory. You cannot directly learn that from video data.

items.question: Why do you favor collecting first-person video for robot learning when third-person video on YouTube is so abundant?
items.object: First-person versus third-person video data for robot learning
items.answer: Fundamentally, there are two points. One is fidelity versus scalability. How scalable a dataset is and how much useful signal it has are, to a large extent, not things you can optimize both at once. For example, third-person data is extremely scalable: you can download it directly from YouTube. But it is extremely difficult to process as a data source, because our current understanding is that the distributions of human and robot data need to be as similar as possible. Extracting from all of YouTube the portion of data that happens to align with robot data is extremely difficult. Truly normalizing it and making the distributions the same is even harder. So the amount of data you can actually use is very small. By contrast, if we really ask people to collect first-person-perspective data, that is not so difficult, given good equipment and many people who want to do it.

items.question: What do you think determines the limits of a robot learning sports skills from first-person human data?
items.object: The limits of robots learning sports skills from first-person human data
items.answer: I think the boundary may depend on how good the third layer is: how well our robot embodiment can control itself to attain the states humans demonstrate—the ability to achieve those control targets. For example, if a human throws a ball 30 meters and I know the end-effector velocity, then if my robot can accurately trace that end-effector velocity or acceleration, I think it can be done. But if you can do that, it is actually a hard problem. Still, if it can be done, I do not think learning basketball from a first-person perspective is far off. Of course, there are many other problems. First-person perspective is a partially observed problem because there are hand signals such as tactile haptics that we are not yet capturing. But assuming we capture everything we can about the ego—the human embodiment's data—I do not think doing basketball is impossible.

items.question: How do you distinguish the world-model approach from treating humans as a source of behavioral-cloning data?
items.object: World-model and behavioral-cloning approaches to human data
items.answer: There are now two completely different understandings of human data in 2026. One is the world-model approach: I only need to know what the next frame of the world looks like. The second is to use humans as another type of robot, treating humans as another source of BC data. These two ways of using human data are completely different. In the first, I only need first-person visual data—video data. In the second, I need human actions and all inputs, including tactile signals: the input-output relationship of humans as an equation. items.question: How do you understand the importance of tactile data for robotic manipulation?
items.object: Tactile data for robotic manipulation
items.answer: I think it will be the second most important type of data. I think video data is still the most important. Then there is a data modality that I have not studied systematically enough: wrist cameras. Namely, what is the relationship between this and tactile? Imagine you have a camera mounted on your wrist, and it sees the interaction between your hand and the object. It solves a major class of problems with egocentric video. When you are holding something in egocentric video, it may be largely occluded by your own hand. But if you have a camera on your wrist, you can see what your hand is doing. Once you have that camera, how much tactile data do you still need? I have never been very clear on that. Tactile is definitely extremely important, because I have a theory: all agents, or all robots and humans, are essentially force-exertion engines. Your purpose in this world is to exert force on the world. That force changes the state of the world, right? So what matters most is not measuring tactile; it is measuring force—how much force you actually exert on something. Tactile is only the most direct, imperfect measurement of force.

items.question: Why do you think cloning human behavior for robots is so difficult?

items.answer: It is a filtering problem, right? There is also a lot of modeling... If you really think carefully about how do you behavior clone a human, it is extremely, extremely difficult. Do we need to clone that action? All of these things make behavior-cloning an agent extremely, extremely difficult. I think this is also different from autonomous driving.
